group: Revised Cardiac Risk Index for Pre-Operative Risk
question:
Patient note:
A 72-year-old woman was seen this morning in the pre-operative medicine suite five days before a scheduled pylorus-preserving pancreaticoduodenectomy for a 2.3-cm pancreatic head mass detected on contrast-enhanced MRI during evaluation of painless jaundice; the hepatobiliary surgeon anticipates an extended upper midline incision with Kocher maneuver, resection of the gallbladder, distal stomach, proximal duodenum, and pancreatic head, reconstruction with pancreaticojejunostomy and hepaticojejunostomy, an operative duration of six to eight hours, expected blood loss of 400–700 mL, and immediate postoperative admission to the surgical intensive care unit for hemodynamic monitoring and nasojejunal feeding. The patient arrived by taxi from her apartment, opted to climb one flight of stairs rather than use the elevator, and conversed comfortably during the five-minute hallway walk to triage, noting that at home she still prepares meals, tends a small herb garden on her balcony, and is able to vacuum the living room without stopping, though she becomes winded if she attempts to carry a heavy laundry basket up two flights. Her past history is notable for an embolic left parietal lobe infarct three years ago that presented with transient word-finding difficulty and right-hand clumsiness; deficits resolved completely after ten days of inpatient rehabilitation, and she has remained on aspirin 81 mg daily and high-intensity rosuvastatin without further neurologic events. She denies any episodes of chest tightness, arm or jaw discomfort, exertional light-headedness, palpitations, or prior coronary testing, and has never been hospitalized for fluid overload or cardiomyopathic symptoms. Hypertension was diagnosed in her late fifties and is well controlled on amlodipine 5 mg each morning and lisinopril 10 mg nightly, with home logs averaging 126/72 mm Hg. Type 2 diabetes was recognized seven years ago during a routine physical when fasting glucose measured 132 mg/dL; lifestyle modification with 45-minute brisk walks five evenings per week and metformin extended-release 1000 mg at dinner have kept her most recent hemoglobin A1c at 7.1 %, and she has never required injectable therapy. Stage 3a chronic kidney disease, attributed to a combination of hypertensive and diabetic microvascular changes, is co-managed with nephrology every six months; serum creatinine has ranged from 1.4 to 1.7 mg/dL over the past two years without albuminuria. Hyperlipidemia is treated with the aforementioned statin. There is no history of chronic lung disease, asthmatic symptoms, peripheral arterial claudication, valvular heart disease, connective-tissue disorders, or abdominal aortic aneurysm. Surgical history consists only of an uncomplicated laparoscopic appendectomy at age 21. She never smoked, enjoys a five-ounce glass of red wine on Sundays, and denies recreational drug use. Family history is pertinent for a brother who experienced a thrombotic stroke at 68 and a mother who died of colon cancer at 79; no first-degree relatives suffered premature myocardial infarction. Review of systems today is negative for fever, chills, productive cough, orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, ankle edema, unintentional weight change beyond the nine pounds lost intentionally through a dietitian-guided low-fat regimen, melena, or easy bruising. After five minutes sitting quietly, vital signs recorded on the right arm were blood pressure 118/68 mm Hg, regular pulse 72 beats per minute, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 98 % breathing ambient air, oral temperature 36.6 °C; body mass index calculated at 26 kg/m². She appeared comfortable and oriented, with clear speech and no residual aphasia. Jugular venous pulsation was not elevated, carotid upstrokes were brisk without bruit, and the point of maximal impulse was located in the fifth interspace at the mid-clavicular line. Cardiac auscultation revealed crisp S1 and S2 without gallop, click, or pathologic murmur. Lungs were resonant to percussion with vesicular breath sounds throughout and no adventitious noises. Abdominal examination disclosed mild right upper-quadrant tenderness to deep palpation, a palpable non-tender gallbladder, no ascites, and active bowel sounds; no hepatosplenomegaly was detected. Extremities were warm with 2+ radial, dorsalis pedis, and posterior tibial pulses, and there was no pitting edema or digital clubbing. Neurologic screening showed full orientation, intact cranial nerves, symmetrical 5/5 strength, normal sensation to light touch and vibration, and a steady narrow-based gait. Laboratory studies drawn one hour before the visit demonstrated hemoglobin 12.9 g/dL, hematocrit 38 %, white blood cell count 6.8 × 10⁹/L, platelet count 242 × 10⁹/L, sodium 139 mmol/L, potassium 4.4 mmol/L, chloride 103 mmol/L, bicarbonate 23 mmol/L, blood urea nitrogen 28 mg/dL, and serum creatinine 1.66 mg/dL, corresponding to an estimated glomerular filtration rate of approximately 45 mL/min/1.73 m²; fasting plasma glucose in the same sample was 128 mg/dL, aspartate aminotransferase 42 U/L, alanine aminotransferase 38 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 320 U/L, total bilirubin 2.4 mg/dL with direct fraction 1.6 mg/dL, and international normalized ratio 1.0. A twelve-lead electrocardiogram obtained today displayed normal sinus rhythm at 74 beats per minute, PR interval 160 ms, QRS 96 ms, axis 50°, and no ST-segment deviations or pathologic Q waves compared with a tracing six months earlier. Upright postero-anterior chest radiography showed clear lung fields, normal cardiac silhouette, and no pleural effusion. Airway assessment by anesthesia revealed a Mallampati class II view, inter-incisor distance 4 cm, thyromental distance 6.5 cm, and full cervical extension. The anesthetic plan includes continuation of beta-blocking and renin-angiotensin system agents on the morning of surgery, half-strength bowel purgative the preceding evening, thoracic epidural placement for post-operative analgesia, balanced general anesthesia with low tidal-volume ventilation, radial arterial and central venous catheters, point-of-care glucose monitoring with subcutaneous correction only if values exceed 200 mg/dL, judicious crystalloid guided by stroke-volume variation, and avoidance of nephrotoxic medications. Pneumatic compression devices, subcutaneous heparin beginning the night of surgery, incentive spirometry, early ambulation, and speech-language evaluation for postoperative swallow safety were discussed in detail; the patient demonstrated accurate teach-back regarding medication timing and nil-per-os instructions and expressed understanding of the risks of bleeding, pancreatic fistula, delayed gastric emptying, wound infection, deep-vein thrombosis, neurologic, pulmonary, and renal complications, and affirmed her desire to proceed with the planned operation in hopes of curative resection.

Question: What is the patient's score of the Revised Cardiac Risk Index for Pre-Operative Risk? You should use the patient's medical values and health status when they were first admitted to the hospital prior to any treatment.
solution:
The Revised Cardiac Risk Index assigns one point for each of six preoperative factors:
- High-risk surgery: planned pancreaticoduodenectomy is intraperitoneal → 1.
- Ischemic heart disease: no documented history → 0.
- Heart failure: no documented history or clinical findings → 0.
- Cerebrovascular disease: prior ischemic stroke counts despite complete neurologic recovery → 1.
- Preoperative insulin treatment: diabetes treated with metformin, not insulin → 0.
- Preoperative creatinine >2.0 mg/dL: measured creatinine 1.66 mg/dL → 0.
Sum = 1 + 0 + 0 + 1 + 0 + 0 = 2.
Final answer: 2
